questions.q: Which finding distinguishes obstructive sleep apnea from central sleep apnea?
ch: Continued respiratory effort against an obstructed airway
questions.exp: OSA maintains respiratory effort despite upper-airway collapse.

questions.q: Which screening tool considers a score >=3 high risk?
questions.exp: STOP-BANG is the standard screening questionnaire.
Polysomnography is the confirmatory test.
An AHI of 5-15 defines mild OSA.
CPAP is first-line.

ch: Uncomplicated adults with high pretest probability
questions.exp: Home sleep apnea testing is reserved for uncomplicated high-probability adults.
Alcohol relaxes airway muscles.
Oxygen does not relieve airway obstruction.

questions.q: Selected CPAP-intolerant patients may benefit from:
questions.exp: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is an option in appropriate candidates.

questions.q: Untreated OSA is strongly associated with:
questions.exp: OSA contributes to atrial fibrillation recurrence and cardiovascular risk.

questions.q: Which diagnostic procedure is the cornerstone for evaluating a new unexplained pleural effusion?
questions.exp: Diagnostic thoracentesis allows pleural fluid analysis.
They distinguish exudates from transudates.
Ultrasound improves safety.
Chylothorax is classically milky.
Pleural fluid causes dullness to percussion.
CHF is the classic transudative cause.
Empyema requires drainage plus antibiotics.
Pleurodesis is used to reduce recurrence.
Hemorrhagic fluid raises concern for hemothorax or malignancy.
Management is etiology-directed.

questions.q: Elevated calcium with inappropriately normal PTH suggests?
questions.exp: An inappropriately normal PTH in the face of hypercalcemia indicates primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.q: Most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?
questions.exp: About 85% are single adenomas.
A low calcium/creatinine clearance ratio suggests familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.

questions.q: Rapid bridge therapy for severe hypercalcemia?
questions.exp: Calcitonin lowers calcium rapidly.
Hypercalcemia shortens the QT interval.
Cortical bone is preferentially affected.
Restore volume first.
Hematuria is not part of the stones/bones/groans/moans mnemonic.
Rapid bone remineralization causes hungry bone syndrome.
Thiazides raise serum calcium.

questions.q: Which combination is required to diagnose metabolic syndrome?
questions.exp: Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when any 3 of 5 criteria are present.

questions.q: Which process is considered the central pathophysiologic driver of metabolic syndrome?
questions.exp: Insulin resistance drives the syndrome.

questions.q: Which lipid abnormality is most characteristic?
questions.exp: The classic dyslipidemia is high triglycerides with low HDL.

questions.q: Which physical finding suggests insulin resistance?
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans is strongly associated with insulin resistance.
Modest weight loss improves all components.

questions.q: Medication class with weight-loss and cardiometabolic benefit?
ch: GLP-1 receptor agonists / dual GIP-GLP-1 agonists
questions.exp: These agents improve weight and cardiometabolic risk.
MASLD commonly accompanies metabolic syndrome.

questions.q: Approximate increase in type 2 diabetes risk?
questions.exp: Risk is about fivefold.

questions.q: Best marker of chronic glycemic control?
questions.exp: HbA1c reflects the prior 2-3 months.

ch: Treat each risk factor and emphasize lifestyle modification
questions.exp: Treat overall cardiovascular risk and each component.

questions.q: Which laboratory profile best defines HHS?
ch: Glucose >600 mg/dL, effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, minimal ketones, pH >7.30
Glucose >250 mg/dL with marked ketones and pH <7.30
questions.exp: This combination is the classic diagnostic fingerprint of HHS.

questions.q: What is the first treatment priority?
questions.exp: Restore intravascular volume before insulin.

questions.q: Mental status correlates most closely with:
questions.exp: Neurologic dysfunction tracks effective serum osmolality.
HHS typically affects older adults with type 2 diabetes.
Residual insulin suppresses ketogenesis.
Giving insulin before checking potassium risks worsening hypokalemia.
Infection is the most common precipitant.
HHS causes profound dehydration, typically 5-10 L.

questions.q: Major complication of overly rapid correction:
questions.exp: Avoid rapid osmolar shifts, which risk cerebral edema.

ch: Give SC basal insulin with overlap
questions.exp: Overlap with subcutaneous basal insulin prevents rebound hyperglycemia.

ch: Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with concentrated urine and high urine sodium
questions.exp: SIADH classically produces euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia with concentrated urine and high urine sodium.
Small-cell lung cancer is the classic malignant cause.

questions.q: First-line therapy for chronic mild-to-moderate SIADH?
questions.exp: Fluid restriction is first-line.
Vaptans antagonize V2 receptors.

questions.q: Initial treatment for seizures from SIADH?
questions.exp: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia requires hypertonic saline.

questions.q: Best discriminator from cerebral salt wasting?
questions.exp: SIADH is euvolemic; cerebral salt wasting is hypovolemic.

ch: Low uric acid and low-normal BUN
questions.exp: Low uric acid and low-normal BUN support SIADH.
Correcting faster than recommended risks osmotic demyelination.
SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Treat the underlying trigger whenever possible.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man reports producing 7 liters of urine daily and drinking water constantly. Which mechanism best explains diabetes insipidus?
ch: Impaired AVP (ADH) production or renal response causing inability to concentrate urine
questions.exp: Diabetes insipidus results from dysfunction of the AVP axis. Either AVP is deficient (central DI/AVP deficiency) or the kidney is resistant to AVP (nephrogenic DI/AVP resistance), so the collecting duct cannot concentrate urine.
why: Insulin excess causes hypoglycemia, not hypotonic polyuria.
Aldosterone primarily regulates sodium and potassium handling rather than aquaporin-2 insertion.
Glucose-mediated osmotic diuresis is a mimic that should be excluded and is not DI.
Increased ANP is not the defining mechanism of DI.

questions.q: Which laboratory profile is most consistent with untreated diabetes insipidus?
ch: Low serum osmolality with concentrated urine
High urine osmolality with low serum sodium
High serum osmolality with urine osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg
Low serum sodium with concentrated urine
questions.exp: Untreated DI classically produces a high serum osmolality with inappropriately dilute urine. Urine osmolality is often below 300 mOsm/kg, and urine specific gravity is typically below 1.005.
why: DI causes dilute, not concentrated, urine.
Urine osmolality is low in DI and sodium may trend upward if water losses are not replaced.
This pattern is more consistent with SIADH.
DI usually produces a very low urine specific gravity.

questions.q: After a water-deprivation test, urine osmolality rises by more than 50% following desmopressin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A marked rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin shows that the kidney can respond to AVP. This localizes the defect to inadequate AVP secretion, which is central DI.
why: Primary polydipsia reflects excessive water intake rather than AVP deficiency.
Nephrogenic DI shows little or no concentrating response to desmopressin.
SIADH causes concentrated urine before desmopressin.
Hyperglycemic osmotic diuresis is not classified by the desmopressin response.

questions.q: Which medication is first-line therapy for central diabetes insipidus?
questions.exp: Desmopressin is a synthetic AVP analog and the first-line treatment for central DI. It may be given intranasally, orally, or parenterally and should be titrated to the lowest effective dose.
why: Thiazides are mainly used for nephrogenic DI.
Amiloride is preferred for lithium-induced nephrogenic DI.
NSAIDs are adjunctive therapy in nephrogenic DI.
Loop diuretics do not treat central DI.

questions.q: A patient taking lithium develops nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Which medication is specifically preferred?
questions.exp: Amiloride blocks ENaC in collecting-duct cells, reducing lithium entry and helping restore concentrating ability. It is the preferred option for lithium-induced nephrogenic DI.
why: Acetazolamide is not the preferred therapy for lithium-induced DI.
Spironolactone does not specifically block lithium entry through ENaC.
Furosemide would worsen water loss.
Mannitol causes osmotic diuresis.

questions.q: Which MRI finding is classically associated with central diabetes insipidus?
ch: Loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot on T1-weighted imaging
questions.exp: Loss of the normal posterior pituitary bright spot on T1-weighted MRI is a classic clue to central DI and reflects loss of normal vasopressin storage in the posterior pituitary.
why: Ventricular enlargement is not a classic DI finding.
Empty sella can occur in other pituitary disorders but is not the classic DI clue.
Pineal calcification is unrelated.
Temporal-lobe edema is not characteristic of DI.

questions.q: Which modern laboratory approach is increasingly replacing the traditional water-deprivation test?
questions.exp: Copeptin is a stable surrogate for AVP. Measurement after hypertonic saline or arginine stimulation can distinguish central DI, nephrogenic DI, and primary polydipsia more reliably than the traditional water-deprivation test.
why: ACTH testing evaluates adrenal function.
BNP evaluates cardiac stretch and heart failure.
Renin testing assesses the renin-angiotensin system.
Aldosterone testing does not classify DI.

questions.q: A patient with diabetes insipidus becomes lethargic and develops seizures after losing access to drinking water. Which complication is most likely?
questions.exp: Unreplaced free-water loss in DI can cause severe hypernatremia. Neurologic manifestations include lethargy, confusion, seizures, and coma, making this a medical emergency.
why: DI is unrelated to glucose metabolism.
Hyperkalemia is not the typical acute electrolyte complication.
Hypercalcemia may cause nephrogenic DI but does not explain this acute presentation.
Severe hypernatremia, not acidosis, is the characteristic danger.

questions.q: A patient receiving desmopressin develops headache, nausea, confusion, and seizures. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Excess desmopressin combined with excess free-water intake can produce dilutional hyponatremia and water intoxication. Headache, nausea, confusion, and seizures are warning signs.
why: Undertreated DI more often causes hypernatremia and ongoing polyuria.
Hyperglycemia does not result directly from desmopressin.
Hypercalcemia does not explain this desmopressin-associated syndrome.
The symptom pattern in this context is most consistent with acute hyponatremia.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes diabetes insipidus from SIADH?
ch: Diabetes insipidus produces dilute urine, whereas SIADH produces concentrated urine
SIADH typically causes polyuria with hypernatremia
questions.exp: DI and SIADH are mirror-image water-balance disorders. DI produces inappropriately dilute urine and tends toward hypernatremia, whereas SIADH produces inappropriately concentrated urine and tends toward hyponatremia.
why: DI produces dilute urine.
Neither disorder is defined by hypoglycemia.
SIADH usually causes water retention and hyponatremia rather than polyuria and hypernatremia.
Untreated DI tends toward hypernatremia, not hyponatremia.
